content: An ellipse, derived from the Greek word ἔλλειψις meaning absence, is a geometric figure defined as the set of all points in a plane such that the sum of the distances from any point on the ellipse to two fixed points, called foci, remains constant. Alternatively, an ellipse can also be described as the path traced by a point that maintains a constant ratio (less than one) between its distance from a fixed point (focus) and its distance from a straight line (directrix) that does not pass through the focus. An ellipse is a type of conic section. It is formed when a conical surface is intersected by a plane that does not cut through the base of the cone. The resulting curve at the intersection is an ellipse. This can be demonstrated using the concept of Dandelin spheres. Algebraically, an ellipse is represented in the Cartesian plane by a quadratic equation where the coefficients are real, and the equation has more than one solution, defining pairs of points (x, y) on the ellipse. An ellipse can be constructed using two pins, a loop of string, and a pencil. The pins are placed at the foci, and the string is looped around the pins and the pencil. By keeping the string taut and moving the pencil around, the sum of the distances from the pencil to the two pins remains constant, thereby tracing the shape of an ellipse. The longest line segment that passes through the foci and terminates on the ellipse is called the major axis. The line segment perpendicular to the major axis, passing through the center of the ellipse (the midpoint between the foci), and terminating on the ellipse is called the minor axis. The semimajor axis is half the length of the major axis, extending from the center to the edge of the ellipse along the major axis. Similarly, the semiminor axis is half the length of the minor axis. If the two foci coincide, the ellipse becomes a circle, which is a special case of an ellipse with zero eccentricity. An ellipse centered at the origin can be viewed as the transformation of a unit circle under a linear mapping associated with a symmetric matrix. The axes of the ellipse align with the eigenvectors of the matrix, and the eigenvalues correspond to the lengths of the semimajor and semiminor axes. An ellipse can also be generated by stretching a circle along one axis, effectively scaling the x-coordinates of all points on the circle while keeping the y-coordinates unchanged. The shape of an ellipse is characterized by its eccentricity, denoted by ε. Eccentricity is a non-negative number less than one, representing the constant ratio of the distance of a point on the ellipse from a focus to its distance from the corresponding directrix. An eccentricity of zero indicates that the ellipse is a circle. For an ellipse with semimajor axis (a) and semiminor axis (b), the eccentricity is calculated as (ε = sqrt{1 (b^2/a^2)}). The greater the eccentricity, the more elongated the ellipse becomes. The linear eccentricity, denoted as (c), is the distance from the center to either focus, and the distance between the two foci is (2c). In polar coordinates, an ellipse with one focus at the origin can be expressed by the equation (r = frac{a(1 ε^2)}{1 + ε cos θ}), where (r) is the radial distance, (θ) is the angle, and (ε) is the eccentricity. The semilatus rectum, denoted as (l), is the distance from a focus to the ellipse along a line perpendicular to the major axis. It is related to the semimajor and semiminor axes by the formula (l = b^2/a). The area enclosed by an ellipse is given by (πab), where (a) and (b) are the lengths of the semimajor and semiminor axes, respectively. The circumference of an ellipse, denoted as (C), is approximately (4aE(ε)), where (E(ε)) is the complete elliptic integral of the second kind. The arc length of a portion of the ellipse's circumference can be calculated using an incomplete elliptic integral. An ellipse retains its geometric properties under uniform stretching along any axis, whether within or outside its plane. Such transformations may alter its eccentricity or axis lengths but preserve its classification as an ellipse. Similarly, an oblique projection of a circle onto a plane results in an ellipse, provided the projection forms a closed curve. Ellipses exhibit a unique reflection property. If a light source is placed at one focus of an elliptical mirror, all reflected rays converge at the other focus. This property is also observed with sound waves, making elliptical rooms ideal for acoustic phenomena. For example, a person standing at one focus of a whispering gallery can clearly hear another person speaking at the other focus. In physics, ellipses play a significant role. Johannes Kepler's first law of planetary motion states that planets orbit the Sun in elliptical paths, with the Sun at one focus. Isaac Newton later explained this as a consequence of his law of universal gravitation. In a two-body system with negative total energy, the orbits of both bodies are ellipses with a common barycenter at one focus. In optics, the index ellipsoid describes the refractive index of anisotropic materials as a function of direction. In computer graphics, drawing an ellipse is a common operation supported by standard display libraries such as the Macintosh QuickDraw API, Windows GDI, and Windows Presentation Foundation. Efficient algorithms for rendering ellipses, such as those developed by Jack Bresenham and Jerry Van Aken, use integer arithmetic to calculate points on the ellipse. These algorithms are widely implemented in modern graphics systems.
